title: API Inspector Training in the USA: 510, 570, 580 and 653 Prep
description: Self-paced online exam prep for API 510, 570, 580 and 653 with instructor Q&A. Compare the four exams, eligibility and which certification to take first.
h1: API Inspector Training in the USA: Exam Prep for API 510, 570, 580 and 653
html:
API inspector training: what the four API certifications cover

The American Petroleum Institute runs its Individual Certification Programs (ICP) for people who inspect equipment in refineries, chemical plants, terminals and pipeline systems. Four of those programmes shape most in-service inspection careers in US downstream oil and gas: API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for process piping, API 653 for aboveground storage tanks and API 580 for risk-based inspection. API 510, API 570 and API 653 hold ANSI accreditation. Each of the four is a three-year credential that API issues after an examination delivered by Prometric: API 510, 570 and 653 are sat in person at a test centre, while API 580 can be taken at a centre or by remote proctoring.

This page compares the four exams, explains how API counts experience, suggests an order for collecting them and describes who hires API inspectors in the United States. Atlantis provides an exam-preparation course for each of the four. Each course is self-paced and online, with instructor Q&A. API decides who is eligible, administers the examination and certifies the candidates who pass; a course prepares you for that examination and never stands in for it.

API 510, 570, 580 and 653 compared

The three inspector codes share one examination format and one eligibility scale; API 580 tests how a risk-based inspection programme is built and run.

CertificationWhat it certifiesEquipmentEligibility in briefExamination
API 510 Pressure Vessel InspectorKnowledge of in-service inspection, repair, alteration and rerating of pressure vessels under API 510Columns, drums, reactors, separators and exchanger shells, most built to ASME Section VIII Division 1A degree, diploma or none, matched with one to five or more years of qualifying vessel experience gained in the last 10 years170 questions, 110 closed-book and 60 open-book, across a 7.5-hour day
API 570 Piping InspectorIn-service inspection, rating, repair and alteration of metallic piping under API 570Process piping in refineries and chemical plants, most of it built to ASME B31.3The same scale, with the experience in pipingThe same 170-question, two-part day as API 510
API 653 Aboveground Storage Tank InspectorInspection, repair, alteration and reconstruction of atmospheric storage tanks under API 653Welded and riveted steel tanks built to API 650 or its predecessor API 12C, in refineries, terminals and pipeline tank farmsThe same scale, set out in Annex D of API 653, with the experience on tanksThe same 170-question, two-part day
API 580 Risk Based InspectionUnderstanding of risk-based inspection as described in the API 580 Body of Knowledge, which draws on API RP 580Whole programmes: risk ranking, inspection planning, data quality and reassessmentAutomatic for holders of a current 510, 570 or 653; otherwise education plus one to five or more years of petrochemical experience90 multiple-choice questions, closed-book, 3.25 hours

On the inspector exams, 140 of the 170 questions are scored and 30 are unscored pretest items that API is trialling; you cannot tell which is which. The day opens with a short tutorial, then 2.75 hours of closed-book questions, a 45-minute lunch break and 3.75 hours of open-book questions. You bring no papers, notes or books. For the open-book half the code documents are provided as PDF files on the test computer, which means search technique matters as much as memory. API 580 is shorter: 80 of its 90 questions are scored, the whole paper is closed-book, and API sets a passing scaled score.

How API counts education and experience

For API 510, API 570 and API 653, eligibility is a trade between formal education and years of relevant experience. The experience has to fall within the last 10 years, and API's wording ties it to work done while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency. The application asks you to document it and API verifies it.

  • Bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology (or three or more years of technical military service): one year supervising or performing inspection activities on the equipment the code covers.
  • Two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology (or two years of technical military service): two years in design, construction or fabrication, repair, operation or inspection of that equipment, of which one year is supervising or performing inspection.
  • High school diploma or equivalent: three years of the same experience, again with one year in inspection.
  • No formal education: five or more years of the same experience.

A dishonorable discharge removes the military route. API 580 uses a simpler scale based on petrochemical industry experience in the last 10 years, and skips it altogether for anyone with a current API 510, 570 or 653. The exact wording, with worked cases, sits on the API 510 certification, API 570 certification and API 653 certification explainers; check there before you decide which window to apply for.

The detail that catches people is that the experience is equipment-specific: three years of thickness readings on piping circuits describe piping work, not tank work. Describe the duties you performed and the equipment you performed them on, in terms the person who signs your experience record can confirm.

Which API certification should I get first?

Start with the code that matches the equipment you already inspect. Because the experience requirement is tied to that equipment, the first certification usually chooses itself once you look honestly at your last few years of work.

  • Refinery or chemical plant unit inspector, mostly on piping circuits and CMLs: API 570 first. Piping is where the volume of in-service inspection sits on most process units.
  • Turnaround internal inspections on columns, drums and exchangers: API 510 first. Vessel entries, internal visual inspection and thickness surveys are the core of the 510 body of knowledge.
  • Terminal, tank farm or pipeline company with breakout tanks: API 653 first. Tank owners in those businesses often need a 653 inspector on staff or under contract.
  • Inspection planner, reliability engineer or RBI team member: API 580 can come early, but most people add it after one of the three inspector certifications because a current 510, 570 or 653 makes them eligible automatically.

The second certification is often the other half of the vessel and piping pair, since refinery roles cover both. Several references, such as API RP 571 on damage mechanisms, API RP 577 on welding and ASME Section V and Section IX, have typically appeared in more than one Body of Knowledge, so the second exam builds on reading you have already done. Each exam still has its own code, its own calculations and its own Publications Effectivity Sheet. For a longer decision guide see API 510 vs 570 vs 653: which certification first, the API inspector certification guide and API 510 vs API 570 compared.

Who employs API inspectors in the United States

The employers follow from a definition in API 510. An authorized inspection agency can be the inspection organisation of the jurisdiction where the vessel is used, the inspection organisation of an insurance company that writes pressure vessel insurance, the inspection organisation an owner or user maintains for its own equipment, or an independent organisation or individual under contract to and under the direction of an owner or user. API 570 and API 653 work on the same principle. In practice that produces four groups of employers.

  1. Owner-users. Refiners, petrochemical and chemical producers, gas processors, terminal operators and pipeline companies run their own inspection departments. EIA counted 130 operable US refineries at the start of 2026, with about 18.2 million barrels per calendar day of crude distillation capacity, and each one needs an inspection programme for its vessels, piping and tanks.
  2. Inspection contractors. Companies that supply inspectors to owner-users, from single-site resident teams to crews that follow turnaround season from region to region.
  3. Insurers and jurisdictions. Some boiler and machinery insurers and some state and city programmes employ inspectors, although their work leans towards boilers and National Board commissions.

Two federal rules keep the demand steady. OSHA's Process Safety Management standard requires inspection and testing on covered process equipment to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices (29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4)(ii)), and refiners and chemical operators commonly point to the API inspection codes as theirs. For hazardous liquid pipelines, PHMSA's 49 CFR 195.432 requires atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to be inspected according to API Std 653, and tanks built to API Std 2510 according to section 6 of API Std 510. That is why pipeline companies hire tank inspectors. The risk-based inspection in the USA page covers the owner's side.

The API inspector career path

Few people start out as API inspectors. Most arrive from NDT, welding, operations or engineering.

  • NDT technicians with ASNT Level II certifications in UT, MT, PT or VT often spend years taking the readings that inspectors evaluate, then move across. See NDT training in the USA for the ASNT SNT-TC-1A route.
  • Welders and welding inspectors bring fabrication and repair knowledge; many hold the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential first. Atlantis runs a six-day AWS CWI exam-prep course for that step.
  • Operators and maintenance technicians bring unit knowledge that counts towards the operation and repair side of the experience scale.
  • Engineers with a bachelor's degree reach eligibility fastest, needing one year of inspection activity.

After the first certification, inspectors widen their scope. The second inspector code is common. API also runs supplementary programmes in the same ICP family: API 571 Corrosion and Materials (automatic eligibility for current 510, 570 or 653 holders; 110 closed-book questions in 3.25 hours), API 577 Welding Inspection and Metallurgy, API 936 for refractory personnel, API 1169 for pipeline inspectors, the source inspection programmes for fixed, rotating and electrical equipment, and the QUTE programmes that qualify ultrasonic examiners for manual, phased array and thickness measurement work. Later roles include lead inspector, inspection supervisor, RBI specialist and mechanical integrity manager, where API 580 matters more.

API inspector salary: what moves the pay

Published averages blend very different jobs, so here is what tends to move pay rather than a figure that will date.

  • Certificates held. A second inspector code makes you useful on more of a unit.
  • Staff or contract. Staff roles trade rate for steady employment; contract roles often pay more per hour with gaps between jobs.
  • Turnaround hours and travel. Long turnaround shifts, rotation work and per diem can outweigh the base rate.

For figures and their sources see the API 570 inspector salary guide and the NDT inspector salary page.

Preparing for more than one API exam

Each inspector exam mixes closed-book knowledge of the code's rules with open-book questions that send you into the referenced documents, and each has a calculation family of its own. API 510 candidates work with required thickness for shells and heads, maximum allowable working pressure, corrosion rate, remaining life and pressure test values. API 570 candidates work with piping corrosion rates over long and short terms, remaining life, inspection intervals and pressure design thickness under ASME B31.3. API 653 candidates work with shell minimum thickness, bottom and annular plate remaining thickness, settlement and hydrostatic test considerations. API 580 has little arithmetic; it tests concepts such as probability of failure, consequence of failure, inspection effectiveness and when a risk assessment must be updated.

Study the code editions named on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window, not the edition your plant uses; edition changes cost well-practised inspectors marks. The course pages for each exam, linked below, go through the content code by code, and the API 510, API 570 and API 653 practice question pages give a feel for the question style.

After the exam: the three-year term and recertification

API 510, 570 and 653 certifications run for three years. You can apply to recertify from 90 days before the expiry date, and there is a 90-day grace period with late fees. To recertify without sitting the full exam again, you must have spent at least 20% of your time in the last three years performing or supervising inspection of the equipment the certification covers, and you report 24 hours of continuing professional development per three-year cycle across at least two categories. Every six years there is also a web-based quiz on code changes: 25 open-book questions in four hours, pausable up to three times, one retake allowed. API 580 also runs on a three-year term with the same 90-day window and grace period, and employment verification is not currently required to recertify it.

Employers sponsoring API candidates

Employers often enrol several inspectors at once, for example to widen certificate coverage before a turnaround season. Fees are quoted on request, and a sponsored group can mix candidates preparing for different exams. Each candidate still applies to API individually, so the most useful early step is to help candidates document their experience accurately: duties, equipment and dates, signed by someone who supervised the work. Owners who need NDE and data review on their equipment rather than training can look at the API 510, 570 and 653 inspection guides; Atlantis performs UT, MT, PT and VT in the US and leaves inspector-of-record decisions with the owner's authorized inspector.

faq.a: API ICP stands for the American Petroleum Institute's Individual Certification Programs. They certify individuals, not companies, against API codes and recommended practices. The best known are API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping, API 653 for aboveground storage tanks and API 580 for risk-based inspection. API sets eligibility, administers each examination through Prometric (in person for API 510, 570 and 653; at a centre or remotely proctored for API 580), issues the certificate and manages recertification. Training providers, including Atlantis, play no part in the certification decision.

faq.q: Is the Atlantis API exam-prep course approved by API?
faq.a: No. Atlantis is not an API-approved, API-accredited or API-endorsed training provider, and the course does not grant any API certification. It is an independent exam-preparation course, self-paced online with instructor Q&A, built around the Body of Knowledge API publishes for each window. You apply to API yourself, API checks your education and experience, and you sit the examination through Prometric, at a test centre or, for API 580 only, by remote proctoring where API offers it.

faq.q: Do I need to work for an authorized inspection agency to qualify?
faq.a: For API 510, API 570 and API 653, API's wording ties the qualifying experience to work done while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, within the last 10 years. An owner-user's own inspection department counts as one, as does a contractor working under an owner's direction. If unsure, read the eligibility text on the certification pages and describe your duties accurately; API verifies the experience.

faq.q: Can I take API 580 without holding API 510, 570 or 653?
faq.a: Yes. Holding a current API 510, 570 or 653 makes you eligible for API 580 automatically, but it is not the only route. Without one of those certifications you qualify through education plus petrochemical industry experience in the last 10 years: one year with a bachelor's degree, two years with a two-year degree, three years with a high school diploma and five or more years with no formal education. The API 580 examination is 90 closed-book questions in 3.25 hours.

faq.q: Which API exams are open book?
faq.a: API 510, API 570 and API 653 each have a closed-book part of 110 questions and an open-book part of 60 questions. For the open-book part the code documents are provided as PDF files on the test computer; you cannot bring your own books, notes or tabs. API 580 is entirely closed-book. Open-book does not mean easy: time per question is limited, so finding answers quickly has to be practised.

faq.q: How long is the API inspector exam day?
faq.a: For API 510, 570 and 653 the day is 7.5 hours: a short tutorial, 2.75 hours for the closed-book questions, a 45-minute lunch break and 3.75 hours for the open-book questions. API 580 is a single 3.25-hour closed-book session. API runs each exam in set windows during the year, each with its own application deadline; the exam schedule page lists the current windows.

faq.q: Can my company sponsor several candidates?
faq.a: Yes. Employers can enrol several candidates, including candidates preparing for different API exams, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies at their own pace with instructor Q&A and applies to API individually. Tell us which examinations and windows your candidates are aiming for when you enquire.
